implementation_notes: Scala mud is usually one sbt module with a package-per-feature layout that has no real dependency discipline, aggravated by the implicits: an implicit val defined in a package object is available to everything that imports it, which is a global dependency with no import statement to grep for. Diagnosis has to account for that — an import graph alone misses implicit edges. Consolidation means sbt modules (compiler-enforced, since sbt forbids project cycles) plus narrowing implicit scope to explicit parameters; the compiler's `-Xsource:3` and scalac options for unused warnings help keep the surface honest.
idiom_name: one sbt module; implicits + typeclasses reaching everywhere
pitfalls: Implicits in scope from a package object are invisible to every import-graph tool, so mud can hide entirely in the type system.
sbt's `aggregate` references make projects build together without a real code dependency, which confuses every measurement of the build graph.
A `trait Foo` with a companion `implicit val` as the default provider means the graph has edges that only exist under `-Xsource` resolution.
